rv.q: The show can’t recover from this intensity; certainly, we cannot.
There's so much to cherish in this miracle of a musical, its puzzle-box structure, thematic patterning, and its shocking release.
This Caroline, Or Change is a hurricane wind unleashed on decrepit legacies and newfound cautions.
The chance to believe in change is her hard-won bequest to them — and, in this devastating, uncomfortable, crucial musical, to us.
It is the unblinking yet compassionate portrait of the title character that lifts the show into the sublime.
Sharon D Clarke's towering performance as Caroline anchors this revival, bringing both volcanic power and devastating vulnerability to Kushner's complex character study.
Leander Deeny’s supercharged characterisation is devilishly good.
Caroline, or Change is a masterwork, even in its altered frame.
In the end, the production is clearly saying that Caroline’s existential struggles in this riven, deeply unfair America can be rationalized only as a gift to the next Black generation.

Caroline's tragedy resonates with a force that takes hold of you by the guts, even more so as Emmie closes the show on a promise of hope, proudly declaring herself the daughter of a maid who repudiates fear.
The result is a show that, despite its considerable musical and dramatic strengths, feels more like a well-intentioned lecture than a fully realized work of musical theater.
Director Michael Longhurst’s entire lethargic production, brought here from Britain, denies her the snowballing buildup that would ensure a big payoff in the end.
“Caroline, or Change” ought to be better appreciated today.
This production stakes a claim for the musical as an essential classic, iconic in both its scope and execution.
The collision of musical styles and Kushner’s clever, witty lyricism makes Caroline, Or Change a haunting, unforgettable musical.
It’s not easy to juggle despair and exuberance without resorting to sentimentality, and Caroline still manages the task handily.

That song and its show-stopping performance is a few minutes that, pardon the pun, will be life-changing for many of the people lucky enough to experience it.
Longhurst's revival is strongly sung, led by the astounding vocals of Sharon D. Clarke in the title role.
Longhurst’s staging, supplemented by Ann Yee’s minimal choreography, is exceptional.
It is an excellently constructed show, its message surviving mostly intact.
It all makes for one massive scrambled egg of a narrative.
I believed in next to nothing of what I saw in this revival.
All the performers are better than the script.

cn.t: Critics hail this timely revival as a triumph, with Sharon D Clarke's towering performance anchoring Kushner and Tesori's ambitious, deeply moving musical about race and class in 1963 Louisiana—though a few find it overly didactic.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
